Six math clues · answer key

A Kitchen Sponge

Age 8 / Grade 2 math. Compare tens and ones. For rounding, locate the two nearby tens; a halfway value rounds up. Welcome spoken reasoning or a number line.

Math 1 · 47
32 < 47. The greater amount is 47 millilitres.
Math 2 · 60
63 rounds to 60. It is 3 away from 60 and 7 away from 70.
Math 3 · 58
58 > 51. The greater amount is 58 millilitres.
Math 4 · 30
25 rounds to 30. Halfway counts round up to the next ten.
Math 5 · 89
76 < 89. The greater count is 89 drops.
Math 6 · 100
97 rounds to 100. It is 3 away from 100 and 7 away from 90.
Age 8 / Grade 2 math. Three two-digit comparisons and three nearest-ten rounding tasks. Rounding is a requested extension. A ones digit of 5 rounds up. The comparison answer key gives the greater number and the completed comparison. These story quantities are practice data, not measurements of the paintings or sponge capacity.

WONDER DAILY AGE 8 · GRADE 3 · ANSWERS · 2 / 3

Reading & writing · answer key

A Kitchen Sponge

Reading · 1
Water entered the connected spaces inside the sponge, clinging to the walls and spreading through narrow gaps.
Reading · 2
A squeeze makes the spaces smaller and pushes water out. When Big lets go, the sponge springs back and its spaces open again.
Reading · 3
Use same-size pieces of the same kind of sponge, equal amounts of water, and the same time. Compare how much water is left in each spill.
Writing
Accept a sensible command, spoken, dictated, or written. Example: “Dip the sponge in the water, then squeeze it over the empty cup.”
Age 8, Grade 3 reading, and Grade 2 math. Lead the optional water test with a new, clean sponge, not the used dish sponge. Use a tray, two clear cups, a measuring cup or spoon, and water. Dip, lift, squeeze over a cup, and compare amounts. Wipe up drips so floors stay dry. Water enters connected pores through wetting and capillary action; cellulose fibres also take up water. Damp cellulose often wets faster than bone-dry cellulose, but materials vary. Compare same-size pieces of the same material, equal water, and equal time. For uptake speed, compare water left in the dishes. Water squeezed from a damp sponge includes water already present, so cup volume alone is not a fair measure of newly absorbed water. The diorama shows qualitative levels during one short dip, not millilitres, capacity, or guaranteed results. It keeps a small amount of water in the sponge after squeezing. Most kitchen sponges are manufactured from cellulose or foam; sea sponges are animals.

Welcome speech, dictation, invented spelling, or writing. One clear command is enough. Example: “Dip the sponge in the water, then squeeze it over the empty cup.”

WONDER DAILY AGE 8 · GRADE 3 · ANSWERS · 3 / 3

Four water clues

A Kitchen Sponge

Quiz 1. Where does water go when a kitchen sponge absorbs it?
Water enters connected spaces inside the sponge. It clings to the walls and creeps into narrow gaps.
Quiz 2. Why does squeezing send water into the cup?
Squeezing makes the spaces smaller and pushes water out. Releasing the sponge lets it spring back open.
Quiz 3. How can Little compare soaking speed fairly?
Use same-size pieces of the same kind of sponge, equal amounts of water, and the same time. Compare the water left in the spills.
Quiz 4. Which statement describes most kitchen sponges?
Most kitchen sponges are made by people from cellulose or foam. Many sea sponges are simple animals.
